name: Animal Farm
blurb: George Orwell's fable of farm animals whose revolution is taken over by the pigs
title: Animal Farm Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: Animal Farm summary: the rebellion, Snowball and Napoleon, the windmill and the final scene explained, chapter by chapter, with who each animal stands for.
h1: Animal Farm: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Animal Farm is a short novel by the British writer George Orwell, first published in England on 17 August 1945 and subtitled A Fairy Story. The animals of Manor Farm drive out their careless owner, Mr Jones, and set out to run the farm themselves as equals. It is told as a simple animal fable, but it is a political allegory of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the rule of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union. The story follows what becomes of the animals' revolution as the pigs take control.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: Old Major
An old prize boar whose dream inspires the animals to rebel
Napoleon
A large, fierce-looking boar who rarely speaks at meetings but knows how to get his way
Snowball
A lively, inventive pig and a persuasive speaker
Squealer
A small, fast-talking pig who explains the leaders' decisions to the other animals
Boxer
An enormously strong, loyal cart-horse who believes hard work solves everything
Clover
A motherly mare and Boxer's companion
Benjamin
An old, cynical donkey who can read but rarely says what he thinks
Mollie
A vain white mare who loves ribbons and sugar
Moses
A tame raven who tells the animals about a paradise called Sugarcandy Mountain
Mr Jones
The drunken, neglectful owner of Manor Farm

body: Chapters 1–2: the Rebellion. Old Major gathers the animals in the barn and tells them that humans steal the products of their labour and kill them when they are no longer useful. He teaches them the song Beasts of England and dies three nights later. The pigs, the cleverest animals, turn his ideas into a system called Animalism. One day Mr Jones gets drunk and forgets to feed the animals, and they break into the store-shed and chase him and his men off the farm. They rename it Animal Farm and paint Seven Commandments on the barn wall, ending with the rule that all animals are equal. Soon afterwards the milk and windfall apples quietly go to the pigs, which Squealer says they need for brainwork.

Chapters 3–5: Snowball and Napoleon. Jones returns with men to retake the farm, but the animals, led by Snowball, defeat them in what they call the Battle of the Cowshed. Mollie runs off to pull a cart for a human. Snowball and Napoleon disagree on everything, above all Snowball's plan to build a windmill to generate electricity. On the day of the vote, nine large dogs that Napoleon has secretly raised from puppies chase Snowball off the farm. Napoleon abolishes the Sunday debates and announces that the pigs will make all decisions; soon after, he claims the windmill was his idea all along.

Chapters 6–8: the windmill and the purges. The animals work longer hours on less food to build the windmill. Napoleon starts trading with humans through an agent, Mr Whymper, and the pigs move into the farmhouse. When a storm knocks down the half-built windmill, Napoleon blames Snowball. Animals confess at a meeting to plotting with Snowball and are killed on the spot by the dogs. Beasts of England is banned. The Commandments change one by one: no animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets, kill another animal without cause, or drink alcohol to excess. Napoleon sells timber to the neighbouring farmer Mr Frederick, who pays in forged banknotes and then attacks, blowing up the windmill. The animals drive the men off at great cost, and the pigs celebrate it as a victory.

Chapters 9–10: Boxer and the years after. The animals rebuild the windmill a second time. Boxer, older now and injured, collapses while working on it. A van takes him away; Benjamin reads the lettering on its side and shouts that Boxer is going to the horse slaughterer, but it is too late. Squealer claims Boxer died in hospital and the van had been bought by a vet; soon after, the pigs buy more whisky. Years pass, most of the animals who remember the Rebellion die, and the farm grows richer, but only the pigs and dogs benefit.

One day the pigs come out of the farmhouse walking on their hind legs, Napoleon carrying a whip, and the sheep, trained to bleat slogans, change their old cry about four legs to say that two legs are better. Clover asks Benjamin to read the barn wall: the Seven Commandments have been replaced by one line, "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others." Napoleon invites neighbouring farmers to a dinner, announces that the farm will again be called Manor Farm, and drinks with Mr Pilkington. A quarrel breaks out when Napoleon and Pilkington both play an ace of spades at cards. The animals looking in through the window turn from pig to man and back again and can no longer tell which is which.

The ending says plainly that the revolution has come full circle: the pigs now rule the other animals as Jones did, and often more harshly. Orwell's own aim is well documented. In a letter to the writer Dwight Macdonald he called the pigs keeping the milk and apples the turning point of the story, suggesting the revolution was lost when the other animals let their leaders take privileges unchallenged. Readers commonly match Old Major to Marx and Lenin, Napoleon to Stalin, Snowball to Trotsky, Jones to Tsar Nicholas II, Frederick to Hitler's Germany and Pilkington to the Western powers. The final quarrel over cards is often read as Orwell's prediction that the alliance between the Soviet Union and the West would not last. Many also read it as a warning that any revolution can be betrayed by those who seize power in its name.

ul: Power and corruption: the pigs begin as leaders of an equal society and end as rulers indistinguishable from the humans they overthrew.
Propaganda: Squealer's speeches, invented statistics, songs and slogans keep the animals working and stop them questioning.
Rewriting history: the Commandments are quietly altered and Snowball's past is rewritten, so the animals doubt their own memories.
Exploited loyalty: Boxer's faith in hard work and in Napoleon makes him the farm's most valuable worker and its saddest victim.
Totalitarianism: one leader rules through fear, the dogs as secret police, staged confessions and control of information.
Length: ten short chapters, usually about 100 pages; it can be read in an afternoon.
Background: Orwell wrote it in 1943–44; several publishers refused it while Britain and the Soviet Union were wartime allies.
Adaptations: a 1954 British animated film (which changes the ending so that the animals rise up against Napoleon) and a 1999 live-action television film.
Content: executions and violence against animals, not graphic.
What teachers usually ask about: who each animal represents, how the Commandments change, Squealer's role as propagandist, why Boxer's fate matters, and what the last scene means.

options: He wins a vote to banish him
He sells him to Mr Frederick
He has his secretly raised dogs chase Snowball off the farm
check.why: On the day of the windmill vote, Napoleon's nine dogs drive Snowball away for good.

He retires to a field on the farm

check.why: Benjamin reads the van's lettering: it belongs to a horse slaughterer.

check.q: What does Napoleon rename the farm at the end?
check.why: He tells the human visitors the farm will go back to its original name, Manor Farm.

faq.q: Who does Napoleon represent in Animal Farm?
faq.a: Napoleon is usually read as Joseph Stalin, who took control of the Soviet Union after Lenin's death, drove out his rival Trotsky (Snowball) and ruled through secret police, show trials and propaganda.

faq.q: What are the Seven Commandments of Animal Farm?
faq.a: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy; whatever goes upon four legs or has wings is a friend; no animal shall wear clothes, sleep in a bed, drink alcohol or kill any other animal; and all animals are equal. The pigs later alter several.

Orwell was a democratic socialist, and the book's target is Stalin's dictatorship and the way the Russian Revolution was betrayed, not the idea of equality itself. He wanted to show Western readers that Stalin's Soviet Union was no model to admire.
